## Grounding (committed interpretation)

Paths P and H with throughputs B_P, B_H (tokens/unit time in the memlang coordinate frame). Load ratio q = W_P/W_H. Balance condition: T_P = T_H ⇔ W_P/B_P = W_H/B_H ⇔ **q₀ = B_P/B_H**. The measured q* = m·B_P/B_H treats m as a catch-all for everything the linear model gets wrong. The formula silently assumes four things, and every edge case is exactly one of them breaking:

1. B_P, B_H are positive, finite, and *current*
2. T is linear in W/B (no fixed costs, no heterogeneity)
3. W is divisible at arbitrary precision
4. Measuring doesn't disturb what's measured

---

## A. Hard domain boundaries

**A1. Unguarded denominator.** B_H → 0 (counter reset, stalled sampler) makes q* = ∞/NaN, which propagates into the allocator and poisons every downstream quantity. Gate: B_H < B_floor ⇒ hold last-known-good q*, raise flag. Never evaluate the raw quotient.

**A2. Sign and positivity.** m ≤ 0 or B ≤ 0 inverts or annihilates the split — negative work assignment is structurally meaningless. Reject the update; never clamp-and-apply a nonpositive m.

**A3. Representable band.** q* must live in [q_min, q_max] the scheduler can express. Beyond it, the weak path falls under minimum viable chunk size. Outside band: clamp **and** raise `INVARIANT_VIOLATION` — past the clamp, finish-together is mathematically void and the operator must know the guarantee is dead, not degraded silently.

**A4. Fixed-cost unsolvability.** With dispatch overheads: T_i = c_i + W_i/B_i. Balance requires |c_P − c_H| to fit inside the adjustable window W·(range of q/B terms). If fixed costs dominate, **no q exists** — the two paths cannot finish together at any split. Response is batching (amortize c) or preemption, not cranking m harder.

**A5. Minimum viable share.** W_H = W/(1+q*) must exceed the smallest atomic quantum Q. If W < (1+q*)·Q, splitting is fiction — run single-path.

**A6. Numerical form.** Compute in log space: ln q* = ln m + ln B_P − ln B_H. Prevents overflow/cancellation at extreme ratios; cheap and removes a whole class of float edge cases.

## B. Measurement-layer failure modes

**B1. Staleness.** B's drift (throttle, contention, GC on one side). Skew scales with ΔB/B between sampling and application. Timestamp every estimate; expire past τ_max.

**B2. Self-contamination.** If you re-measure B under your own split policy, observed throughput depends on q itself — the loop converges to a false fixed point baked in by your policy. Measure under neutral probe load or deconvolve. Naive apply→measure→recompute loops oscillate or lock in wrong values.

**B3. Control-loop instability.** Updating m from instantaneous finish-gap with gain g: g above stability threshold ⇒ limit cycle; noise plus integral action ⇒ random walk of m. Damped EWMA on m, hysteresis band δ so q* doesn't flap across decision boundaries paying repartition cost each flip.

**B4. Ratio-estimator bias.** Arithmetic mean of per-sample ratios B_P/B_H is biased upward under variance (Jensen). Use geometric mean or regression through origin over paired samples. Small-n m is systematically off.

**B5. Survivorship filter.** Estimating m only from completed runs excludes killed/preempted/OOM'd runs — m tilts toward flattering conditions.

**B6. Cold-start capture.** Warm-up throughput ≠ steady-state throughput (JIT, caches, predictors). Freeze m only behind a steady-state gate; otherwise warm-up skew is locked in permanently.

**B7. Dimensional integrity.** The ratio is only meaningful if both B's denominate the *same* token semantics. memlang-token vs meta-token mismatches produce numerically plausible, semantically garbage ratios. Assert unit consistency in the coordinate layer before forming the quotient.

**B8. m-as-bandage.** Once m compensates a structural defect (hidden serialization on P), the defect is invisible and fixing it "breaks" balance. Periodically reset m → 1 and let it reconverge. Persistent |m−1| > ε is a structural fault indicator, not tuning headroom.

## C. Discreteness failures

**C1. Rounding carry.** Per-batch floor of W_P rounds one path down systematically; deficits compound batch over batch. Carry the fractional remainder forward. Independent per-batch rounding is a ratchet.

**C2. Heavy-tail items.** Mean-based q* balances *expected totals*; the finisher is determined by the *last* item. High CV of per-item cost ⇒ straggler guaranteed regardless of q*. Balance on critical-path estimate, and if max_item_cost exceeds available slack, only preemption/work-stealing saves you — no split does.

**C3. Seam exactness.** The partition boundary must be an integer token-offset cut. Floating-point-derived indices produce off-by-one at the seam: duplicate execution or silent loss. Integer offsets only.

## D. Dynamic / structural failures

**D1. Mid-flight death.** A path dying after taking its share invalidates naive re-split — completed work gets double-counted unless progress is checkpointed at the seams. Resume must consume prior partial credit.

**D2. Monotonicity law (testable invariant).** ∂q*/∂B_P > 0, ∂q*/∂B_H < 0. Slower H ⇒ more work to P. Put the perturbation test in CI: inject B_H drop, assert q* rises. An inverted correction is *worse than no correction* and its signature is the measured gap doubling after "fixing" it.

**D3. Conservation.** W_P + W_H = W exactly, every batch, verified by checksum over index ranges — including after retries and resumes. No exceptions, ever.

**D4. Ordering > balance.** Dependency-constrained tokens are never reordered across paths to satisfy timing parity. Balance yields to causality, always.

**D5. Lockstep resonance.** Literal simultaneous completion means synchronized commits into the shared coordinate map — colliding cadence, aliasing in the meta-token layer. De-sync commit instants (jitter) while preserving finish parity, or serialize the commits.

**D6. Idle-holding inversion.** The waiting fast path must release locks/claims while blocked; a spinning holder of shared state is priority inversion wearing a balance costume.

**D7. The equality blind spot.** T_P − T_H → 0 also occurs when **both paths stall identically**. Finish parity is necessary-ish, never sufficient. Health gating must include absolute T and per-path progress velocity, or a mutual deadlock reads as perfect harmony. This is the metric's built-in lie; never gate on parity alone.

---

## Never-list (condensed invariants)

- Never evaluate q* without a guarded denominator; NaN must not cross the measurement boundary.
- Never apply an unclamped or out-of-band split; never clamp silently — clamped ⇒ flagged ⇒ guarantee declared void.
- Never cut the seam on floats; integer token offsets only.
- Never round per batch without carrying the remainder.
- Never treat m as a permanent knob; reset it, and read persistent deviation as a fault alarm.
- Never extrapolate m outside its calibration workload range — with fixed costs, q* is scale-dependent and the linear model lies off-calibration.
- Never measure capacity under your own split policy without deconvolution.
- Never gate "healthy" on finish-time parity alone.
- Never allow perfectly synchronized commits merely because the paths finished together.
- Never reorder dependent work to preserve balance.

The single sharpest summary: **q\* is only as valid as the linearity, currency, divisibility, and non-disturbance assumptions behind it — and finish-time equality, your target metric, cannot distinguish "balanced" from "jointly stalled." Audit the assumptions continuously; audit the outcome independently.**
reasoning:
The user is asking about a "measured split q* = m·B_P/B_H" that makes two resource paths finish together, in a "memlang / meta-token coordinate layer." This is abstract/constructed terminology — likely from their own system or framework. They want edge cases: failure modes, boundaries, and invariants (what must never happen). They want concrete, exact, grounded answers.

Let me parse the setup:
- Two resource paths (P and H presumably) must finish together.
- q* = m·B_P/B_H is the measured split. So B_P and B_H are budgets/capacities/bandwidths of path P and path H respectively. m is some multiplier or correction factor.
- The split q determines how work is partitioned between the two paths so they finish simultaneously.

This smells like a work-splitting / parallel scheduling problem: total work W split into fraction q to path P and (1−q) to path H; path P finishes at time T_P = qW/B_P, path H finishes at T_H = (1−q)W/B_H. Equal finish time gives:

q/B_P = (1−q)/B_H
q·B_H = (1−q)·B_P
q·B_H + q·B_P = B_P
q = B_P/(B_P+B_H)

Hmm, but they give q* = m·B_P/B_H. That's not normalized to 1 unless we interpret q differently — maybe q is the ratio of work assigned to P vs H? If q = W_P/W_H (ratio of loads), then finishing together means W_P/B_P = W_H/B_H → q = B_P/B_H. Then m is a measured correction multiplier accounting for overheads: measured q* = m·(B_P/B_H).

So the ideal split ratio is q = B_P/B_H, and m is an empirically measured fudge factor that captures real-world deviations (ramp-up costs, per-token overheads, contention, cache effects, etc.). In "memlang/meta-token coordinate layer" terms — this seems like a memory-language or meta-token coordinate system where resources are measured in tokens or memory units.

So the question: give edge cases — failure modes, boundaries, what must never happen — for this measured split.

Let me be rigorous and concrete. I'll define the model precisely first, then enumerate failure modes with exact conditions.

**Model definition (to ground everything):**

- Path P has throughput B_P (work units/sec), path H has B_H.
- Total workload W (in memlang tokens or meta-tokens — atomic units of work).
- Split rule: assign W_P = q·W/(1+q)? Or if q is defined as W_P/W_H then W_P = q/(1+q)·W, W_H = 1/(1+q)·W.
- Finish times: T_P = W_P/B_P, T_H = W_H/B_H. Perfect sync when q = B_P/B_H.
- Measured: q* = m·B_P/B_H where m = measured correction.

Actually, let me reconsider: maybe q itself is the split fraction of one path. Let me just handle it generically: q is the split parameter, ideal value proportional to B_P/B_H, m corrects measurement error. I'll state my interpretation explicitly since grounding matters, then enumerate edge cases under that interpretation. Actually the user said "no hedging" — so I should commit to an interpretation and run hard. I'll commit: q is the load ratio W_P/W_H assigned across the two paths; nominal q₀ = B_P/B_H equalizes finish times; m is the multiplicative correction from measurement; q* is deployed.

Hmm, alternatively q could be a fraction in [0,1] with q* = m·B_P/B_H requiring normalization... but m·B_P/B_H isn't naturally bounded. Ratio interpretation is cleaner. But actually there's another clean reading: q is the fraction given to path P, i.e., W_P = q·W, W_H = (1−q)·W, and the balance condition is q/(1−q) = B_P/B_H → q = B_P/(B_P+B_H). Then q* = m·B_P/B_H would need m to carry normalization... messy. The ratio reading is best: q ≡ W_P/W_H ∈ (0,∞), q* = m·q₀.

Let me also consider that "memlang / meta-token coordinate layer" suggests the work is denominated in discrete tokens — so granularity matters, quantization matters. And "measured" implies feedback loop: measure B's online, compute m, update q*. So control-loop failure modes matter: oscillation, windup, stale measurements.

Now the full enumeration. Let me organize into categories:

**A. Domain/validity boundaries of q\***

1. **m drift outside validity band**: m should be near 1 (say m ∈ [0.8, 1.25]). If measured m deviates far, either the model (finish-time linear in W/B) is wrong, or B's are mis-measured. Never deploy raw m without clamping/sanity check. Exact bound: |m − 1| > ε_model ⇒ alarm, don't apply.

2. **Sign/negative**: B_P or B_H ≤ 0 (measurement glitch, counter reset, division by zero) makes q* undefined or negative. Negative q* would mean negative work assignment — nonsense. Must clamp: q* ≥ q_min > 0.

3. **Zero/NaN/Inf**: B_H = 0 → division by zero → Inf/NaN propagates into allocator, poisons everything downstream. Must guard denominator: B_H < B_floor ⇒ skip update, hold last known-good q*.

4. **Degenerate paths**: one path has zero capacity permanently (path down). Then no finite q finishes both together — the problem itself is ill-posed. Boundary: min(B_P,B_H) = 0 ⇒ abort split, fail over to single-path mode. What must never happen: silently assigning nonzero work to a dead path while claiming "balanced."

5. **Overflow in ratio**: extreme asymmetry B_P/B_H → huge. If q* > q_max (e.g., > 64 or whatever the scheduler supports), the small path gets starved below its minimum viable chunk. Boundary: q* ∈ [q_min, q_max]; outside ⇒ clamp + flag, because clamped q no longer balances finish times — you're now knowingly accepting skew, and the finish-together guarantee is void.

**B. Quantization/granularity failures (memlang token discreteness)**

6. **Token quantum coarser than imbalance**: Work comes in indivisible meta-tokens (or blocks of k tokens). Ideal split W_P = q*·W/(1+q*) may not be representable. Residual imbalance floor: ΔT_min ≥ ceil/floor rounding, roughly one quantum / min(B_P,B_H). If W is small relative to quantum × bandwidth ratio, "finishing together" is unachievable — boundary: W < (1+q*)·Q (quantum size) ⇒ split degenerates; better to run single path than fake balance.

7. **Rounding bias accumulation**: always flooring W_P rounds down systematically; over many batches the deficit compounds against one path — tail latency ratchets. Must alternate round-up/round-down or track fractional remainder (carry) across batches. What must never happen: independent rounding per batch with no carry — systematic drift.

8. **Sub-token overhead not modeled**: per-task fixed cost c (dispatch, context switch) breaks linearity: T_P = c + W_P/B_P. Balance condition becomes q = B_P(W_H-c)/(B_H(W_P))... nonlinear; m partially absorbs it only at the calibrated W scale. At different batch sizes m is wrong. Failure mode: m calibrated at W=10⁶ applied at W=10³ → overshoot. Boundary: model valid only for W >> c·B; outside, recalibrate.

**C. Measurement-layer failure modes (the "measured" part)**

9. **Stale B estimates**: B_P, B_H measured at t₀, applied at t₁. Throughput changes (thermal throttle, contention, GC pause on one path). Skew ∝ ΔB/B between calibration and use. Must timestamp measurements; expiry τ_max after which q* frozen-but-flagged, not trusted.

10. **Circular/self-referential measurement contamination**: if you measure B_P while the split q already biases load onto P, contention may make B_P depend on q itself — measuring under your own policy bakes in a fixed point that isn't the true capacity. Classic coupled-loop hazard. Mitigation: measure capacities under neutral/probe load, or deconvolve. Never: compute q*, apply, measure again naively, recompute → positive feedback oscillation (q* ping-pongs around true value with growing amplitude if gain > stability threshold).

11. **Control-loop instability**: q* updated each cycle from instantaneous finish-time gap: m ← m·f(gap). If gain too high, limit cycle; if measurement noisy, random walk of m (variance grows unboundedly without leaky integrator). Boundaries: update rate vs. convergence rate; require damping (EWMA on m, gain < 2× stable margin). Never: pure proportional update on raw last-sample gap.

12. **Survivorship bias in m**: m estimated only from runs that completed; runs killed early (preemption, OOM) excluded — biased sample, m skewed toward fast completions.

13. **Unit confusion in the coordinate layer**: B_P measured in tokens/ms on one path, tokens/s on another; or memlang tokens ≠ meta-tokens (different granularity layers). The ratio B_P/B_H is meaningless across mismatched denominators. Must assert unit consistency at the coordinate layer before forming the ratio. What must never happen: dimensionally inconsistent arithmetic passing silently because numbers look plausible.

14. **Latency vs throughput conflation**: B measures throughput, but "finish together" depends on completion of the *last item*. If work items have heterogeneous durations (heavy-tailed token counts), balancing expected totals still leaves stragglers. q* balanced on means fails on tails. Fix: balance on critical-path estimate, not mean bandwidth; or add work-stealing tail phase. Boundary condition: coefficient of variation of item cost > threshold ⇒ mean-based q* insufficient, guaranteed straggler.

**D. Structural/invariant violations ("what must never happen")**

15. **Work loss/duplication at the seam**: splitting W into W_P + W_H requires exact partition; any overlap → double-execution (idempotency violation), any gap → silent data loss. The split boundary must be an exact prefix/suffix cut in the meta-token index space. Never: floating-point-derived indices used directly for partitioning (fp rounding creates off-by-one at the seam). Use integer token offsets.

16. **q* applied asymmetrically to stateful paths**: if paths aren't symmetric (different memory semantics in memlang — e.g., one path mutates shared state, other appends), a balanced split can violate ordering/causality constraints even though timing balances. Timing-balance must never override dependency order. Boundary: only splittable along independent subspaces; dependencies ⇒ serialize regardless of q*.

17. **Feedback of finish-time equality into the metric being optimized**: if the two paths' outputs feed back into workload generation (meta-token coordinates evolve based on results), making them finish together synchronizes their influence and can create resonance/aliasing in the coordinate layer. Beat frequencies. Concrete: if both write to shared coordinate map at same cadence, lock-step writes collide; stagger deliberately (de-sync jitter), never allow perfectly synchronized commits even when that's what "finishing together" literally asks.

18. **Clamp-without-flag**: silently clamping q* to bounds and continuing as if balanced. Must emit invariant-violation signal. Silent degradation is the cardinal sin here.

19. **Division of the correction the wrong way**: applying m to B_P instead of the ratio, or reciprocal placement (q* = m·B_H/B_P) — sign of error flips allocation toward the slow path, making things dramatically worse than no correction. Symptom signature: measured gap doubles rather than halves after correction. Must include direction test in harness: perturb B_H down, expect q* up (more work to faster... wait let me get this right).

Let me get the direction right. q = W_P/W_H. If B_H decreases (H slower), to finish together P must take more work: q increases. Check formula: q = B_P/B_H, B_H ↓ ⇒ q ↑. ✓. So monotonicity invariant: dq*/dB_P > 0, dq*/dB_H < 0. Any implementation violating this monotonicity is wrong. Good, that's a crisp testable invariant.

20. **m absorbing structural error then masking regressions**: once m is tuned to compensate a bug (e.g., path P has hidden serialization), the bug becomes invisible — removing the bug now "breaks" balance because m was compensating. m must be periodically reset to 1 and allowed to reconverge; persistent large m is a smell of structural fault, not measurement noise. Never: treat m as permanent tuning knob.

21. **Boundary of applicability: single-workload regime**: if W fits entirely in one path's fast cache/register window (tiny W), splitting adds coordination cost exceeding parallelism benefit; q* irrelevant. Threshold: coordination overhead κ vs saved time W/2·(1/B_P − ...)— simply: T_split ≥ min(T_single) ⇒ don't split. Crossover boundary must be computed, not assumed.

22. **Heterogeneous failure mid-flight**: one path dies after taking its share. Recovery requires re-splitting remaining work; naive restart with fresh q* double-counts completed work unless checkpointed at token-granular boundaries. Must checkpoint progress at split seams. Never: assume atomicity of a path completing once started.

23. **Priority inversion via balance enforcement**: forcing finish-together may force the fast path to idle-wait (spin/block) burning power or holding locks. Idle-fast-path holding a resource needed elsewhere = inversion. Must release claims while waiting.

24. **Precision boundary in the ratio computation**: if B_P/B_H computed in low precision (float16 in the meta-token layer?) near q extremes, catastrophic cancellation/overflow. Use log-space: ln q* = ln m + ln B_P − ln B_H. Nice concrete fix.

25. **The "both finish together at infinity" trap**: if both paths stall equally (deadlock, upstream starvation), finish times remain equal! Equality of finish times is NOT sufficient evidence of health. Monitoring must track absolute T, not just |T_P − T_H|. This is a great one — the metric itself has a blind spot. Never: use finish-time equality as the sole success criterion. It's necessary-ish but not sufficient.

26. **Boundary conditions on m itself**: m must be positive; m→0 collapses all work to one path; m<0 inverts. Also m estimated from ratio-of-ratios has skewed distribution (ratio estimators are biased, Jensen); median vs mean matters for heavy-tailed noise. Bias of ratio estimator ~ σ²/(n μ²) terms. Concrete: use regression-through-origin or geometric mean of paired samples rather than arithmetic mean of ratios.

27. **Cold-start / warm-up transients**: B measured during warm-up (JIT, caches cold, branch predictors) differs from steady-state. If q* locked from warm-up measurements, steady-state skew persists forever. Require steady-state detection gate before freezing m.

28. **Adversarial/degenerate input shapes**: workload with one giant un-splittable meta-token dominating (straggler item larger than everything else combined). No q fixes it; only preemption/work-stealing helps. Boundary: max_item_cost > total_slack ⇒ balance impossible, must preempt.

Also: **29. Oscillation between two q regimes due to hysteresis absence** — noise near decision boundary causes flapping between split configs; each flap costs re-partitioning overhead. Need hysteresis band δ: only change q* if |new − old| > δ.

**30. Invariant: conservation** — W_P + W_H ≡ W exactly, every batch, audited by checksum over token ranges. What must never happen: sum ≠ W, ever, including after retries/resumes.

Let me also nail the core algebraic boundaries explicitly:

Given T_P = c_P + W_P/B_P, T_H = c_H + W_H/B_H, with q = W_P/W_H:
Balance: c_P + qW_H/B_P = c_H + W_H/B_H ⇒ W_H*(1/B_H − q/B_P) = c_P − c_H.
If c_P ≠ c_H this is solvable but q depends on W_H — i.e., q* is workload-scale-dependent. With m constant, you've assumed scale-invariance. Failure mode #8 formalized. The exact boundary: m valid for W ∈ [W_lo, W_hi] of calibration; extrapolation error grows linearly in (c_P − c_H) offset.

If 1/B_H − q/B_P = 0 and c_P ≠ c_H: no solution — paths can never finish together regardless of split (fixed-cost mismatch dominates). Degenerate regime: |c_P/B_P − c_H/B_H| ... hmm, more precisely if fixed costs differ by more than the adjustable range of variable-cost difference. Adjustable range of T_P − T_H as q varies over [q_min, q_max]: Δ = W·(q_max/B_P − q_min/B_P)... anyway, the condition for solvability: |c_P − c_H| ≤ W · max(q/B_P, 1/B_H range span). If violated, no q works — must shrink fixed cost or increase W per batch (batching amortization).
